entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ottone Visconti (c. 1207 – August 15, 1295) was the foundational figure of the Visconti dynasty, serving as Archbishop of Milan from 1262 and, crucially, as Lord of Milan from 1277 until his death. His ascent marked a pivotal shift in northern Italian politics, firmly establishing Milan as a Ghibelline stronghold and setting the stage for centuries of Visconti rule. Through a combination of ecclesiastical authority, military prowess, and shrewd political maneuvering, Ottone transformed the communal governance of Milan into a proto-signoria, shaping the city-state's destiny and its role within the Holy Roman Empire's Italian territories.

His path to power was paved by a protracted and brutal conflict against the Guelph Della Torre family, who had dominated Milanese politics for decades. Appointed Archbishop by Pope Urban IV in 1262, a choice contested by the Torriani, Ottone spent years in exile, gathering forces and support from other Ghibelline cities and the imperial faction. The decisive moment arrived on January 21, 1277, when Ottone's forces, led by his nephew Teobaldo Visconti, decisively defeated Napoleone della Torre's army at the Battle of Desio. This victory allowed Ottone to enter Milan triumphantly, imprison Napoleone, and consolidate his authority, effectively ending the Della Torre's hegemony and commencing the Visconti era.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ottone Visconti's victory and establishment of the Visconti dynasty fundamentally altered the political landscape of northern Italy, transforming Milan into a dominant regional power for centuries and influencing the trajectory of the Italian Renaissance.
